core.text: The last and smallest noun family runs on *e*: **a 5th-declension noun (the e-pattern: dies, diei; res, rei)**. *diēs* (day): *diēs, diem, diēī, diēī, diē*; plural *diēs, diēs, diērum, diēbus, diēbus*. The two words that matter are *diēs* and *rēs* (thing, matter); the others are *faciēs* (face), *merīdiēs* (midday), *spēs* (hope), *fidēs* (trust), *glaciēs* (ice). They are feminine — except *diēs* and *merīdiēs*, which are masculine. Latin name: dēclīnātiō quīnta.
A declension is a family of nouns that share one set of endings. This is the fifth and last: after it there are no more noun patterns to learn.
-ēs, -em, -ēī, -ēī, -ē; plural -ēs, -ēs, -ērum, -ēbus, -ēbus; the genitive -ēī marks the family.

invented.en: In summer the days are long.

core.text: *diēs* and *rēs* look like 3rd-declension plurals (*ovēs*, *pānēs*). The dictionary genitive tells them apart: *diēs, diēī* (5th) against *ovis, ovis* (3rd). In a sentence, an *-ēs* form with a singular verb (*diēs est*) is a 5th-declension singular; and only the 5th has *-ēī, -ērum, -ēbus*.

more.text: Only *diēs* and *rēs* have a full plural; most of the others are used in the singular. After a consonant the *-ēī* shortens to *-eī*: *reī, speī, fideī*. *Rēs* is everywhere in idioms: *rēs pūblica* (the state), *rē vērā* (in truth), *quā dē rē* (about which matter).
*diēs* is masculine when it means a day in general, feminine when it means a fixed date or a stretch of time: *diē certā* — on the appointed day. *merīdiēs* is always masculine.

The learner's notes (week 13): in every case but the genitive the pattern matches the *is*-nouns with *e* where they have *e* or *i* (*diēs, diem, diēbus*); the genitive looks like the 2nd declension with an *e* in front (*-eī, -ērum*). Ørberg (chapter XIII) declines *diēs* and adds *merīdiēs* m., *faciēs* and *glaciēs* f. and a few other feminines; *māne* (morning) is an indeclinable neuter that never changes its ending.
